Sleep - The New Wonder Drug

By: Diana Lucas | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Summary:
Scientists have discovered a revolutionary new treatment that makes you live longer. It enhances your memory, makes you more attractive. It keeps you slim and lowers food cravings. It protects you from cancer and dementia. It wards off colds and flu. It lowers your risk of heart attacks and stroke, not to mention diabetes. You’ll even feel happier, less depressed, and less anxious. Its called sleep, what we don’t have enough of,

Chronic sleep deprivation has been called ‘the disease of our time’. A century ago, people slept for an average of nine hours a night, today it is closer to seven hours. Strict schedules of full work or school days, early mornings for exercise, late nights for television or emails all disrupt our circadian rhythms. Sleep is the thing we regularly sacrifice for ‘more important’ activities. The effects of insufficient sleep are horrifying: poor memory, weight gain, low mood, higher anxiety, lower libido, shorter life expectancy. It makes you more likely to get cancer, dementia, Alzheimer’s, diabetes, flu or a cold. You’re more likely to suffer a heart attack or stroke and more likely to die in a car crash. Regularly getting less than seven hours a night is as harmful as smoking or drinking to excess. There is serious evidence that lack of sleep is a factor in the onset of depression and schizophrenia, and is even associated with the symptoms of ADHD.
 


Further information:
A world increasingly filled with blue light from computer screens and televisions is part of the problem. Without artificial light, as the sun sets the ambient light becomes dimmer and more yellow and triggers the body to produce melatonin. When the sun rises, light (including blue light) increases, stopping the production of melatonin. The drop in melatonin causes the body to wake up. The sleep/wake cycle, also known as the circadian rhythm, is responsible for controlling ones’ sleep patterns. A cell in the eye called a melanocytic receptor and discovered in 2005 reads the blue light in the sky and ‘switches’ the body from day to night mode. But when the world around you is flooded with blue light, your body struggles to detect the change from day to night, melatonin production is suppressed, and our bodies are unable to move effectively into sleep mode.
 
We could do an interesting look at the expert views on sleep, how sleep patterns have changed, the sometimes batty cures for insomnia that are out there, the many apps that have sprung up….and also this local innovation that athletes are using to help them combat sleep deprivation and improve performance when they travel.
 
Dr Robert Daniel, a Specialist Ophthalmologist with training in Human Physiology and Neuroscience, became interested in how the switch (which happens in the eye) works for day and night.  So technically, the way that it happens, is there’s a little cell that was discovered in the eye in about 2005.  They always knew about rods and cones, but there is a third one called a melanocytic receptor and this receptor reads only 460 nanometer blue light (which is typically the blue you see in the sky) and that means we now know how our body knows the difference between day and night.

Based his research Dr Daniel created SleepSpec, basically an amber lens that filters out the blue light and encourages the body to produce melatonin. The Lions rugby team have been monitoring players sleep in order to maximise their competitive benefit both in terms of recovery and performance. Last year, when they travelled to New Zealand, they used Sleep Spec and a complicated programme of eating and sleeping that tried to trick their bodies into believing they were still on SA time until after their game – which they won. The Northern Ireland team at the Commonwealth Games also used Sleep Spec and reported great results.

Dr Rob Collins, the Lions doctor, is a firm believer in the power of sleep.  We would interview him and a couple of the Lions players , how important sleep has been to them and the game when they are continually bombarded with the effects of Jet Lag.

Dr Alison Bentley is considered to be South Africa’s sleep guru. We will talk to her about the effects of sleep deprivation, from medical to performance and how sleep or the lack of it has become such an issue as we work and play 24/7 in more and more connected world.

Sleep, the wonder of

V/O 11 sec
We live in a 24/7 world… Working and socialising across time zones lead to stress and health disorders. The pressures of the modern world are sometimes overwhelming.

Link: Scientists have discovered a revolutionary new treatment that makes you live longer, it enhances your memory, it keeps you slim and lowers your food cravings it also lowers your risk of heart disease dementia and diabetes. It also makes you happier
Its called sleep something we don’t get enough of.

Dr Robert Daniel: An adult needs between 7 to 12 hours of sleep per night and somehow we have come to think that the less you sleep the less lazy you are and more productive you are and pride ourselves I can manage on 4 hours a night that’s actually very dangerous.

V/O 8 sec
The whole question of how we sleep and the quality of our sleep is an ongoing passion of eye specialist Dr Robert Daniel.

Robert Daniel: The eye is an extension of brain, so understanding how it process’s light I then became interested in the switch between day and night which is fundamental for sleep.

Around about 2005 we discovered a new retinal receptor and this receptor only responds to blue which is exactly the same as the blue sky.


V/O 12 sec
At sunset, this receptor, which is made up of microscopic cells in the eye, is no longer receiving the intense blue rays from the sun and that tells the body clock to produce melatonin.


Robert : Melatonin is the night time sleep hormone that is fundamental to sleep If you see blue light you cannot make melatonin.
 
V/O 14 sec
Today, with our addiction dependency on smart phones, tablets and other devices, blue light is everywhere, shining into our eyes from the various screens. The effect on our brain is immediate alertness, like a shot of caffeine.

Robert Daniel: So the problem If you have looked at cell phone…you have switched day switch and you cannot make melatonin for the first 2 hours put your head on the pillow an you may go to sleep but you are not going into the deeper phases of sleep.

Pabi: We are living in a way that humans are not really supposed to be living we are not supposed to be on the go as much as we are, we are not supposed to be looking at screens more than we are looking at each other.

Pabi Moloi
Radio and Television Presenter

V/O 6 sec
Power FM presenter and mother, Pabi Moloi, like so many of us, lives on the go.

Pabi: I have a toddler who wakes up at 5 o clock come rain or shine no matter what has happened so I try to spend as much time with him during the day but I finish work at midnight so there is no typical schedule in my life.
Masa: What is your relationship with sleep?
Pabi: I have a very over active mind, high anxiety levels always planning thinking so its always been something I have grappled with and challenged.

LINK : As a journalist I know how easy it is to put sleep on the back burner you go from covering a service delivery protest to a political rally to a media briefing that could be delayed for hours and then still have go to the studio to file the story.

V/O 7 sec
At the Sleep Lab at Wits Medical School the effects of sleep and the lack of it are monitored and researched.

Mthokozisi: In the University for instance we have a culture of not sleeping we are told not to sleep, study it’s the opposite.

V/O 12 sec
Honours graduate Mthokozisi Lala’s paper, ‘The effects of sleep restriction on cognition’ sets out to find what the effects an afternoon nap has on our mental faculties..

Mthokozisi: We recruited 10 healthy participants aged 18 to 30 so we made sure that they have normal sleep patterns we then invited them to spend 6 different nights at the sleep lab.

V/O 12 sec
Their nightly sleeps were restricted, which affected their cognitive functions like working memory. But Mthokozisi found a 30 minute nap had a significant restorative function.

Mthokozisi: Having a nap in the afternoon can actually help reverse all the things that we have seen from sleep restriction in the first four hours or the last four hours of the night.

Pabi: If I take some naps during the day it helps me get through, if I take a power nap high caffeine content and then a quick nap and then you get up and then somehow miraculously its gone through your brain and your mind.

Dr Stella Iacovides I L
Senior lecturer and Sleep researcher
Wits Medical School,

Stella : Currently we are discovering more and more and more the risks lack of sleep is associated with increased risks of cancer cardiovascular disease, increased incidences of stroke heart attack we have only just touched tip of iceberg re why we need to sleep

V/O
In fact studies have shown a correlation between lack of sleep and dementia. During one’s life, toxic by-products build up in the brain which are only released through sleep.

Robert: So if not sleeping enough the toxins are building up and over a period or years they cause damage to brain presents later as dementia… sleeping tablets… depress/supress activity in brain so if brain not active e you are not releasing and it is been show the chronic use of tablets increases the dementia rate by 59 percent its ,massive

Marilyn I want to sleep so badly that I am almost nervous to try and sleep it’s like a vicious cycle am I going to sleep aren’t I going to sleep so I am fearful.

V/O
Financial advisor and marriage officer Marilyn Michau’s sleep became such a problem, she booked into a sleep clinic.

Marilyn: Where they put all kinds of apparatus on you and they measure I stayed there for four days and my average amount of sleep was 2 hrs 45 mins.
Masa: How are you functioning?
Marilyn: That’s what I don’t understand I have more energy than anyone I know.

V/O
Sleep, why we sleep or how we sleep is a hot topic, be it in self help books, medical journals or conferences.

Link: Sleep is such an issue now that meditation apps that help you to fall asleep
are booming…

Marilyn: Every single sleep meditation that we can possibly down load from the internet I can recite them to you which one would you like?

V/O
In search of a perfect night’s sleep in the modern world, Dr Daniel invented Sleepspecs, glasses which cut out the blue light.

Robert Daniel: I realized that having no screen time is not practical today…the trouble is pretty much all our lighting also contains the blue so I designed a lens that cuts out blue light. So what it means is you can now where the glasses and still watch television and look at your cell phone.

V/O
Even the pilot light on the TV can affect your production of melatonin.

Dr Robert Daniel: If I hold it in front of that you can’t see the blue.

V/O
Lions Rugby players Dylan Smith and Dillon Smit know sleep is one of the most important recovery mechanisms for the body, but playing all over the world jet lag takes its toll.

Dillon Smit - 
Lions Scrumhalf
 
Dylan Smith – 
Lions Prop

Dylan Jet lag for us has a massive effect it works with your co ordination you can feel it in your body usually day 3 for me personally.
Dillon: Its got a big effect on your sleeping patterns and your eating metabolism or anything like that.

V/O
Team doctor, Rob Collins, deals with the constant travelling by slowly adapting the team to the new time zone. So in effect the team members need to live in their own time capsule. In 2016 Rob introduced these specs to the team to help with their sleeping patterns.

Rob Collins: What is beneficial with way we have done it so in the last 2 years Swayze has been our coach there has been a complete buy in to the process. Then we have been able move the times of meals in the hotels and times guys were sleeping and use it so whole team is doing it rather than a few. They need to understand the science behind it and then use it properly,

Dylan: I use it about 2 hours before I want to go to bed and then I sleep like a baby.

V/O
It’s conceivable that the Lions’ top performances in contesting three Super 15 finals in a row coincides with their use of this sleep therapy. But how does one explain their inconsistent performances this year?

Dr Robert Daniel: Essential with professional sports people they need that 1 % they are all competing on an equal level and are constantly looking for something that gives them a little edge

V/O AFC Bournemouth/afcbTV’.
Northern Ireland and Bournemouth soccer clubs have picked up Roberts’s invention and use it in their training routines. Another successful South African pioneering on the global stage.

Dr Rob Daniels: The message has spread across the world we have done quiet a bit AC Bournemouth attributed significant improvement in getting proper restorative sleep the whole concept of sleep is far bigger then we ever imagined it’s fundamental to health and normal physiology.

Last year, when they travelled to New Zealand, they used Sleep Spec and a complicated programme of eating and sleeping that tried to trick their bodies into believing they were still on SA time until after their game – which they won. The Northern Ireland team at the Commonwealth Games also used Sleep Spec and reported great results. Dr Rob Collins, the Lions doctor, is a firm believer in the power of sleep. We would interview him and a couple of the Lions players , how important sleep has been to them and the game when they are continually bombarded with the effects of Jet Lag. Dr Alison Bentley is considered to be South Africa’s sleep guru. We will talk to her about the effects of sleep deprivation, from medical to performance and how sleep or the lack of it has become such an issue as we work and play 24/7 in more and more connected world.
